w: Fernando Botero, Medellin's most famous son, and Pedro Nel Gomez anchor the collection at the city's oldest museum -- the first founded in Antioquia and the second in all of Colombia. It sits on Botero Plaza by the old Berrio Park metro stop, so the artist's bronzes greet you outside before his paintings do inside.
s: Medellin's oldest museum, built around Botero
_facts: art museum housing works by Fernando Botero and Pedro Nel Gomez
first museum established in Antioquia department, second in Colombia
located on Botero Plaza near the Berrio Park metro station

w: Twenty-three Botero bronzes -- his signature swollen figures, all curves and mass -- stand in the open on a 7,000 square metre plaza the artist helped fund, donating the works for the museum's 2004 renovation. No glass cases, no ropes: just Medellin's favourite sculptor's work, weathering outdoors.
s: Twenty-three Botero bronzes, out in the open air
_facts: outdoor park displaying 23 sculptures by Fernando Botero
7,000 square metre park surrounded by the Museum of Antioquia and the Palace of Culture
Botero donated the works for the museum's 2004 renovation
located in the Old Quarter of Medellin

w: For decades this was the tallest thing in Medellin, a 1972 skyscraper named for the textile giant that built it -- Coltejer, once the largest textile complex in Latin America, founded here in 1907. The tower still marks the skyline as a monument to the industry that built the modern city around it.
s: Medellin's tallest tower, built by a textile empire
_facts: tallest building in Medellin, completed 1972
tenth-tallest in Colombia as of 2016
named for Coltejer, one of Colombia's most important textile companies
Coltejer founded in Medellin by Alejandro Echavarria in 1907

w: Fourteen hectares hold 4,500 flowers and 139 recorded bird species, but the real draw is the Orchideorama -- a canopy of steel 'flower' modules built specifically to shelter the garden's orchid collection. Named for Joaquin Antonio Uribe, it's a genuine botanical archive disguised as a city park.
s: City garden built around an orchid-shaped canopy
_facts: 14-hectare botanical garden named for Joaquin Antonio Uribe
has 4,500 flowers and 139 recorded bird species
important orchid collection preserved in the Orchideorama

w: Sixteen thousand hectares of eastern Aburra Valley slope, part nature reserve, part pre-Hispanic archaeological site, reached from downtown by metro and then a Metrocable gondola line straight into the hills. Somewhere among the 54 miles of trails and wildflowers, an outdoor food market waits by the cable-car station.
s: A cable-car ride into pre-Hispanic forest and trails
_facts: ecological nature preserve and pre-Hispanic archaeological site
covers 16,000 hectares, 1,760 of natural forest
54 miles of walkable trails
reached from downtown via the Medellin Metro and Metrocable
outdoor food market next to the gondola station

w: An 1892 park turned unofficial town square, where an equestrian Simon Bolivar -- cast in Italy in 1923 -- has watched over Medellin's cathedral and old theatre district ever since. On the first three Sundays of every month, a university symphonic band still plays open-air at 11:15am, exactly as generations before did.
s: Historic park with a monthly open-air symphony
_facts: urban park inaugurated in 1892, named for Simon Bolivar
equestrian statue erected 1923, designed and cast by Italian sculptors
Metropolitan Cathedral of Medellin on the north side, Lido Theater to the southeast
university symphonic band performs open-air on the first three Sundays each month
hosts a traditional market on the first Saturday of each month

w: Ten abstract and modern sculptures by names like Edgar Negret and Otto Herbert Hajek sit scattered at the foot of Nutibara Hill -- the first sculpture park of its kind anywhere in Colombia. Free, open until midnight, and easy to stumble into from the Industriales metro stop without meaning to.
_facts: first sculpture garden of its kind in Colombia
10 modern and abstract sculptures by Colombian and international artists
closest metro station is Industriales
free to the public, open 6am to midnight

w: A 1945 theatre that once shared its address with a billiard hall before a methodical restoration reopened it in 2007 under the city's own management. It seats 1,100 on the southeastern edge of Park of Bolivar, and its programming still runs year-round under Medellin's cultural office.
s: Restored 1945 theatre on Park of Bolivar
_facts: theater located at the southeastern coast of Park of Bolivar
began operating in 1945, restored and reopened in 2007
administered by the Mayor of Medellin
capacity for 1,100 spectators
site previously occupied by La Macarena billiard hall

w: A private mansion turned museum and garden in El Poblado, its nine rooms packed with porcelain, stained glass, antiques and sculpture collected under one roof. The outside garden does as much work as the interior -- a quiet, castle-shaped detour from the district's newer high-rises.
s: A castle-like mansion museum in El Poblado
_facts: museum and gardens in the El Poblado district
permanent exhibitions of porcelain, glass, stained glass, antiques, paintings and sculptures
nine exhibition rooms plus an outside garden

w: South America's largest freshwater aquarium sits inside a science museum modelled loosely on San Francisco's Exploratorium -- 300-plus interactive exhibits plus a 3D auditorium, planetarium and TV studio, all opened in 2008. It's the rare museum built to be touched rather than roped off.
s: Science museum with South America's biggest freshwater tank
_facts: interactive science museum, opened 2008
loosely modeled on San Francisco's Exploratorium
houses South America's largest freshwater aquarium
over 300 interactive attractions plus 3D auditorium, planetarium, TV studio and vivarium

w: Three black, stone-like buildings glow when lit at night, built on a Santo Domingo Savio hillside as part of Medellin's 'library park' social-urbanism push, partly funded by Spain's own development agency. It won a Lisbon architecture prize in 2008, and the Metrocable still delivers visitors right to the door.
s: Award-winning hillside library, reached by cable car
_facts: library park in the Santo Domingo Savio neighbourhood
funded partly by the Spanish Agency for International Development Cooperation
three buildings meant to resemble black stones, illuminated at night
designed by architect Giancarlo Mazzanti
won best architecture award at the 2008 Ibero-American Architecture and Urban Design Biennial in Lisbon
reached via the Medellin Metrocable at the Santo Domingo stop on Line K

w: A 15,000-seat bullring opened in 1945, still standing in a city that has since largely turned bullfighting into a subject for debate rather than a Sunday habit. These days it's as likely to host a concert as a corrida -- one arena, two very different kinds of crowd.
s: 1945 bullring, now doubling as a concert venue
_facts: bullring in Medellin, opened 1945
holds 15,000 spectators
currently used for bullfighting and concerts

w: A 'zen-inspired' park built between 1998 and 2000 with one blunt instruction: take your shoes off. Sand, bamboo, water fountains and green lawn sit beside the Medellin River downtown, expressly designed for adults and children to walk through barefoot -- playful urbanism as public policy.
s: The downtown park you're meant to walk barefoot
_facts: zen-inspired public park funded by EPM, designed by architect Felipe Uribe de Bedout
includes a green area with gardens and bamboo, a sand area and water fountains
created between 1998 and 2000
located adjacent to the Medellin Metropolitan Theatre and the Medellin River

w: Conceived by a Jesuit-school astronomy society led by a scientist known simply as Brother Daniel, this was South America's first computer-controlled planetarium, established in 1984. It anchors the Park of Wishes, a plaza designed to complement its shape -- proof Medellin was chasing the stars early.
_facts: planetarium established October 10, 1984
originally conceived by the Astronomical Society of the College of San Jose, led by Brother Daniel
surrounded by the Park of Wishes, designed by Felipe Uribe de Bedout
Medellin was the first South American city to have a computer-controlled planetarium

n: Rafael Uribe Uribe Palace of Culture
w: A Belgian architect gave Medellin a slice of Gothic Revival, dome and all, named for a Liberal Party general and now packed with archives -- historical, photographic, musical -- plus a library, gallery and a museum room of its own. The dome still doubles as a screening room. Free to walk into, always.
s: Gothic Revival palace stuffed with Medellin's archives
_facts: public building designed by Belgian architect Agustin Goovaerts in Gothic Revival style
named after Rafael Uribe Uribe, a general of the Colombian Liberal Party
designated a national monument of Colombia, freely open to the public
houses historical and photographical archive, music archive, library, gallery and a museum room
large dome used as an auditorium and projection room
